lesson.title: Working Backward on the Tree: Finding P(Cause Given Effect)
lesson.summary: Once a tree diagram is built, you can reverse a conditional probability by comparing one path's probability to the total of every path that reaches the same outcome, which is Bayes reasoning made visual.
lesson.body:
A tree diagram is not just for finding the probability of a full path. It is also the easiest way to reverse a conditional probability, the same kind of reversal you practiced with the natural frequency counting in Bayes intuition. The general procedure is: identify every path that ends at the outcome you are now conditioning on, add up their probabilities to get a new denominator, and then the numerator is whichever one of those paths you actually care about. This is just the definition P(A given B) equals P(A and B) divided by P(B), with the tree doing the work of finding both pieces.

Return to the factory example from the previous section. The tree gave four path probabilities: machine A and defective, 0.018; machine A and not defective, 0.582; machine B and defective, 0.020; machine B and not defective, 0.380. Also recall that the overall probability an item is defective, found by adding the two "defective" paths, was 0.038.

Now suppose you pull a defective item off the line and want to know: what is the probability it came from machine A? That is P(machine A given defective), and by definition it equals P(machine A and defective) divided by P(defective), which is 0.018 divided by 0.038. Carrying out that division, 18 divided by 38 reduces to 9 divided by 19, which is approximately 0.474, or 47.4 percent.

That number is worth pausing on. Machine A makes 60 percent of all items overall, the majority. But once you condition on the item being defective, machine A only accounts for about 47.4 percent of the defective ones, a minority. The reason is that machine B, despite making fewer items, has a higher defect rate, so it contributes more than its size would suggest to the defective pile. You can check the arithmetic by finding the complementary probability the same way: P(machine B given defective) equals 0.020 divided by 0.038, which is 10 divided by 19, or about 0.526, 52.6 percent. Adding 47.4 percent and 52.6 percent gives 100 percent, as it must, since a defective item came from exactly one of the two machines.

The general lesson: to condition on an outcome using a tree, mentally erase every branch that does not lead to that outcome, then treat the surviving paths as your entire world. The probability of any one surviving path, divided by the total probability of all surviving paths, is your answer. This is exactly the reasoning that made the screening test in Bayes intuition surprising, now organized as a diagram instead of a headcount table.
